title: Roast Beef and Yorkshire Pudding
subtitle: British Sunday roast with rib of beef and batter puddings
excerpt: Roast beef and Yorkshire pudding is the centrepiece of the British Sunday roast: a rib of beef roasted until the outside is dark and crusted and the inside is pink, served with airy, crisp puddings made from a simple batter of flour, eggs, and milk. The Yorkshires must be cooked in very hot fat and must not be opened while they rise.
sourceNotes: The combination of roast beef and Yorkshire pudding is one of the most important dishes in British cooking. Roast beef has been the symbol of English prosperity and national character since the 18th century. Yorkshire pudding was traditionally cooked under the roasting meat, catching the fat dripping from the beef. The modern version is cooked in a muffin tin with very hot lard or dripping.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The Yorkshire pudding batter can be made up to 24 hours ahead and refrigerated.
recipe.temperatureNote: Reduce to 180C after initial sear; use 230C for Yorkshires

content.text: The beef needs to come to room temperature before roasting -- remove it from the fridge at least an hour before it goes in the oven. The Yorkshire pudding fat must be smoking hot before the batter goes in -- this is what makes the batter puff immediately on contact. Once the Yorkshires are in the oven, do not open the door for at least 20 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 220C. Rub {{beef-rib}} beef with {{vegetable-oil}} oil, {{salt-table}} salt, and {{black-pepper}} pepper. Place fat-side up in a roasting tin. Roast at 220C for 20 minutes, then reduce to 180C. Continue roasting for approximately 50 minutes for medium-rare (internal temperature 55C) or 65 minutes for medium (internal temperature 62C). Remove from the oven and rest for 30 minutes, loosely tented with foil.
While the beef rests, increase the oven to 230C. Put a 12-hole muffin tin in the oven with a teaspoon of {{vegetable-oil}} oil in each hole. Heat for at least 8 minutes until smoking.

Beat {{plain-flour}} flour, {{eggs}} eggs, {{whole-milk}} milk, and {{salt-table}} salt together until smooth. Pour the batter quickly into the hot tins, filling each hole halfway. Return to the oven immediately. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes without opening the door until puffed and deep golden. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The Yorkshire puddings did not rise
items.cause: The fat was not hot enough, or the oven door was opened too early.
items.fix: The oil must be smoking before the batter goes in. Work quickly -- pour the batter and get the tin back in the oven within 30 seconds. Do not open the door for at least 20 minutes. The cold air deflates the puddings.

content.text: Roast beef is the most symbolic food in English culture. The John Bull figure of 18th century English satire was always shown eating a vast roast beef. The Sunday roast is still one of the most widely eaten meals in Britain, and the combination of beef with Yorkshire pudding is the most traditional form of it. Yorkshire pudding takes its name from the county of Yorkshire in northern England, where it was eaten as a first course to fill diners before the expensive meat arrived.
